intro: Oakland has one old-growth coast redwood left, Old Survivor, about 470 years old by a 1969 ring count, on a cliff in Leona Heights Park that you see from the road. Downtown, in front of City Hall, stands the oak the city moved there in 1917 to honour Jack London. This page also crosses into Berkeley for two trees on the UC campus: a blue gum grove the university thinks is the tallest stand of hardwoods in North America, and a buckeye a 1950s committee wanted cut down.
meta_description: Oakland's old trees: Old Survivor, its last old-growth redwood, the Jack London Oak at City Hall, and the blue gum grove on the Berkeley campus.
question_meta: Oakland's oldest tree is Old Survivor, its last old-growth coast redwood, dated by a 1969 ring count to about 470 years.
question_answer: The oldest tree in Oakland is Old Survivor, the city's last old-growth coast redwood, in Leona Heights Park. A 1969 core sample counted 415 to 420 rings, which makes it about 470 years old today; some coverage says nearly 500. It is an Oakland Designated Landmark, and you see it from the sidewalk on Campus Drive, since there is no trail to the trunk.
question_context:
Old Survivor grows on a steep rocky cliff among younger second-growth redwoods, and its exact spot is deliberately not published, to protect the habitat around it. That is why our pin sits on Campus Drive, opposite Carl B. Munck Elementary School, where you can look across at it, rather than on the tree. The York Trail gives a more distant view. Please keep off the school grounds.

The other three trees are easier. The Jack London Oak stands in Frank H. Ogawa Plaza in front of City Hall, three minutes from 12th Street City Center BART. It came from Mosswood Park in 1917, already about twenty, which puts it somewhere between 120 and 160 years old; the plaza holds other oaks, so look for its 2017 plaque.

In Berkeley, both campus trees are on open university grounds a short walk from Downtown Berkeley BART. The blue gum grove on Strawberry Creek was planted in 1877 or 1882, depending on which university page you read, as a windbreak for a running track. The buckeye in Faculty Glade was already standing in the 1950s; its real age is not documented.

faq.q: Can I walk to Old Survivor?
faq.a: No. There is no trail to the trunk and its exact location is kept unpublished to protect the habitat. You see it from the sidewalk on Campus Drive, across from Carl B. Munck Elementary School, or at a distance from the York Trail.

faq.q: Why is there a Jack London Oak at Oakland City Hall?
faq.a: The city moved a coast live oak from Mosswood Park to City Hall in 1917 to honour Jack London, who had died the year before. Its original plaque went missing for decades, and it was re-dedicated with a new one in 2017.

faq.q: Are the UC Berkeley trees open to visitors?
faq.a: Yes. The eucalyptus grove on Strawberry Creek and the buckeye in Faculty Glade are on open campus grounds, free and with no posted hours, about five to twelve minutes on foot from Downtown Berkeley BART.

faq.q: How old is the eucalyptus grove at Berkeley?
faq.a: Roughly 145 years. One university page says it was planted in 1882 as a windbreak for the old cinder track; a 2010 university news story says 1877.

trees.name: Old Survivor

location.address: Campus Drive opposite Carl B. Munck Elementary School (viewing place), Leona Heights Park, Oakland, CA 94613

trees.story:
Oakland has exactly one old-growth coast redwood left, and it had to be found twice. An Oakland parks naturalist rediscovered it in 1969, growing on a steep rocky cliff in what is now Leona Heights Park, among younger second-growth redwoods. That same year a core sample from Humboldt State gave a ring count of 415 to 420 years, which puts its birth around 1550 and its age now at about 470. Some coverage rounds that up to nearly 500.

The name it carries, Old Survivor, says why it matters. Every other redwood of its generation in the city is gone. In 1980 the city made it an Oakland Designated Landmark.

Its size is a mess in the sources. One gives it 250 feet and a 26-foot diameter, another 93 feet. Neither squares with the other, so we leave the numbers out rather than pick one.

You cannot walk to it, and that is deliberate. There is no trail to the trunk, and its exact spot is kept unpublished to protect the habitat around it. What you can do is look across at it from the public sidewalk on Campus Drive, opposite Carl B. Munck Elementary School, or from a distance on the York Trail. Our pin marks that viewing place, not the tree. Please stay off the school grounds. It costs nothing, and from the sidewalk you are looking at the only redwood in Oakland that was here before the city.
trees.how_to_recognise: You can recognise it as the tallest, scraggliest old redwood on the rocky cliff above Leona Creek, standing out from the younger redwoods around it. It is seen from Campus Drive, across from the school.
trees.access: View-only. The tree stands on a steep cliff on City of Oakland land in Leona Heights Park with no trail to its trunk; its exact spot is not published. It can be seen from the sidewalk on Campus Drive across from Carl B. Munck Elementary School (a plaque is reported at the school parking lot by Wikipedia) and at a distance from the York Trail. Free. Do not enter the school grounds.
trees.transport: AC Transit bus to Redwood Rd / Campus Dr, Oakland Hills; check current route. Roughly 25 to 30 min from downtown Oakland or Fruitvale BART by bus (not verified, check timetable).
trees.verify_notes: Last old-growth coast redwood in Oakland (Yahoo/Bay Nature style coverage, Feb 2026: standing, no direct trails to trunk, exact location withheld to protect habitat). Oakland Designated Landmark, 24 June 1980 (Wikipedia citing City of Oakland landmark list). Rediscovered 1969 by Oakland parks naturalist Paul Covel; 1969 core ring count (Glen Strouse, Humboldt State) 415 to 420 years relative to 1969, so about 470 in 2026; Yahoo says 'nearly 500'; Wikipedia dates it 1549-1554. Conflicts on size: Wikipedia 250 ft / 26 ft diameter, Yahoo 93 ft; both implausible-or-unreconciled, so girth/height left out. Pin is the public viewing place on Campus Dr (iNaturalist research-grade redwood observations 2024-2026 cluster at 37.7945,-122.1721 and at 37.7925,-122.1767); Wikipedia coordinate 37.7928,-122.1748 is the tree area. Alive: recent iNaturalist redwood observations, Feb 2026 news says standing. Flagged: tree itself not individually pinned by design; pin is viewing place.

trees.name: Eucalyptus Grove, UC Berkeley

location.address: Grinnell Natural Area, north bank of Strawberry Creek, UC Berkeley campus, Berkeley, CA 94720

trees.story:
These blue gums were planted to block the wind on a running track. They are now, by UC Berkeley's own reckoning, thought to be the tallest stand of hardwood trees in North America, with some reaching nearly 200 feet.

The Strawberry Creek walking tour run by the campus says the grove went in during 1882 as a windbreak for the old cinder track. A university news story from 2010 puts the planting at 1877 instead. Either way the grove is somewhere between 144 and 149 years old, and the dates belong to the planting as a whole, not to any one trunk. The same tour goes further than the campus map, calling this the tallest stand of this eucalyptus anywhere in the world. That is the university's claim, and we have not seen the measurements behind it.

The grove is not untouched. In 2010 the university removed seven trees it judged hazardous near the west entrance, so what stands is a thinned stand, still dense and still very tall.

You take it in as one place rather than tree by tree. Walk in from the campus west entrance on the Oxford Street side, five to eight minutes from Downtown Berkeley BART, and follow Strawberry Creek. The grove stands on its north bank in the Grinnell Natural Area. It is free and open with normal campus access.
trees.how_to_recognise: You can recognise it as a dense stand of very tall blue gums with peeling bark. It stands on the north bank of Strawberry Creek, next to the Life Sciences Addition.
trees.access: Free; open campus grounds of UC Berkeley, walk-in from the west entrance (Oxford St / University Ave side). No published hours; normal campus access.
trees.transport: BART Downtown Berkeley station, about 5 to 8 minutes on foot to the campus west entrance and the grove.
trees.verify_notes: Owner pages: berkeley.edu campus map says some trees reach nearly 200 ft and the grove is 'thought to be the tallest stand of hardwood trees in North America'; creeks.berkeley.edu (Strawberry Creek walking tour) says planted 1882 as a windbreak for the old cinder running track, tallest stand of hardwood in North America and of this eucalyptus in the world. Conflict: UC news 22 Mar 2010 says planted 1877 and that seven hazardous trees were removed from the grove near the west entrance; so the grove is thinned but standing. Age from 1877/1882 planting documented for the grove, not individual trunks. Alive: iNaturalist observation 2026-10-14 at the coordinate. Coordinate from the campus map pin (Google Maps link on berkeley.edu), grove-level, so approximate. Ensemble is the destination: one place to stand.

trees.name: Jack London Oak

location.address: Frank H. Ogawa Plaza, 14th St and Broadway, Oakland, CA 94612

trees.story:
Oakland dug up an oak of about twenty and replanted it in front of City Hall to honour a writer. Jack London had died in November 1916. In 1917, under Mayor John L. Davie, the city moved a coast live oak from Mosswood Park, where it had been growing for about two decades, and planted it at City Hall in his name, according to the East Bay Express.

It is still there, in what is now Frank H. Ogawa Plaza. The original plaque was not so lucky. It went missing for decades, and only in January 2017, a hundred years after the planting, was the tree re-dedicated and given a new one.

The age is an estimate built on that story. Roughly twenty when moved, it would now be around 130, though nobody recorded when it first went into the ground at Mosswood, so the honest range runs from about 120 to 160 years.

One caution. The plaza holds more than one oak. Wikipedia describes a single large coast live oak at the plaza's centre as the symbol of the city, and the Express describes the Jack London Oak at City Hall, but we have not seen a source that ties the two descriptions to the same trunk. The new plaque is the surest way to know you have the right tree. If you can confirm it, tell us.

The plaza is free and always open, three minutes on foot from 12th Street City Center BART.
trees.how_to_recognise: You can recognise it by the Jack London plaque from its 2017 re-dedication; the plaza holds other oaks too. It stands in Frank H. Ogawa Plaza, in front of Oakland City Hall.
trees.access: Free; open public plaza in front of Oakland City Hall, no hours.
trees.transport: 12th St / City Center BART station, about 3 minutes on foot.
trees.verify_notes: Moved from Mosswood Park, where it had grown about two decades, to City Hall in 1917 to honour Jack London (died Nov 1916), planted under Mayor John L. Davie (East Bay Express, 21 Feb 2017: still standing, original plaque missing for decades, new plaque after 28 Jan 2017 re-dedication). Wikipedia: a single large Coast Live Oak at the plaza centre, 'the symbol of the city' (no planting date there). Secondary (search snippets only, not used): SF Chronicle column says dug up and moved over four days by eight people, source of the city logo; oaklandwiki says city landmark; landmark status NOT confirmed on a fetched page. Age derived: roughly 20 years old at the 1917 move (age at which it was first planted in Mosswood unknown, so broad). Alive: several iNaturalist research-grade coast live oak observations on the plaza to 2026-07-15 (cannot tell which plaza oak each shows, plaza holds other oaks too). Flagged: single credible source for the transplant story, tree-level pin not confirmed; the plaza centre oak is the one Wikipedia describes. Recheck whether 'Jack London Oak' is the central tree before writing.

trees.name: Faculty Glade Buckeye

location.address: Faculty Glade, UC Berkeley campus, Berkeley, CA 94720

trees.story:
In the 1950s a UC Berkeley tree committee wanted this buckeye cut down. One man argued against it, and the buckeye stayed. Seventy years on it is still standing in Faculty Glade, the lawn beside the Faculty Club.

The campus paper, the Berkeleyan, wrote about it in 1995 as an ancient buckeye whose trunk was a structural marvel. In 2023, when a storm damaged a buckeye at the UC Botanical Garden, the campus news service reached for this one as the comparison. An alumni guide to favourite places on campus describes an old, gnarled tree in the glade that looks dead and comes back with new growth every year, though it does not name the species.

How old it is, nobody can yet say with a source in hand. The documented floor is seventy-odd years, because it was already standing, and already argued over, in the 1950s. A planting date is sometimes repeated, but we have not been able to read it on a page that can back it up, so we leave it out. If you know where it comes from, tell us.

Faculty Glade is open campus ground, free with no hours posted, about ten to twelve minutes on foot from Downtown Berkeley BART.
trees.how_to_recognise: You can recognise it as the old, gnarled California buckeye on the slope of Faculty Glade. It stands on the lawn beside the Faculty Club.
trees.access: Free; open grounds of UC Berkeley, Faculty Glade is a public lawn beside the Faculty Club, no hours published.
trees.transport: BART Downtown Berkeley station, roughly 10 to 12 minutes on foot to Faculty Glade.
trees.verify_notes: Berkeleyan 27 Sep 1995: ancient buckeye in Faculty Glade, already standing in the 1950s when a campus tree committee wanted it removed (Robert Cockrell argued against it); trunk described as a structural marvel. UC Berkeley news 28 Mar 2023 refers to the buckeye in Faculty Glade as the comparison for the UC Botanical Garden buckeye. Alumni page (undated, recent): old gnarled tree that looks dead but returns each year with new growth (does not name species). UNVERIFIED lead: a UC CNR page (cnr.berkeley.edu/breakthroughs/wt16/the-big-picture, seen only as a search summary, page did not fetch) says planted 1882, 'seemingly deadened from the inside out but continues to bloom every spring', 'perhaps the best-loved tree on campus'; also on the 'Tall Tree Tales of Cal' campus tour. Do not use 1882 until read on the page. Alive: iNaturalist research-grade California buckeye observations at 37.8730,-122.2617 on 2019-04-26, 2024-04-27 and 2025-07-17 (cluster at Faculty Glade; I could not open the observation text to confirm it is this individual). Pin is the glade area, not the trunk.
